decisions: Should we adopt DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) as the baseline generative model for our image synthesis work, given quality vs compute/sampling tradeoffs?

requirements.description: State the core technical contribution of DDPM: what the forward diffusion process is, what the learned reverse denoising process is, and what this framework enables compared to prior generative models.
Specify the training objective clearly (variational bound / simplified loss) and what the model predicts (e.g., noise/mean/variance), including how timestep conditioning is used.
Describe the sampling procedure end-to-end (reverse diffusion steps): how samples are generated, the number of steps used, and any variance schedule choices that materially affect quality.
Report the main quantitative results from the paper for image generation (e.g., FID / Inception Score and/or NLL/bits-per-dim where applicable) and identify which datasets/benchmarks they are on.
Provide explicit comparisons against key baselines cited in the paper (GANs/flows/autoregressive as applicable): what baselines, what metrics, and whether DDPM is better/worse.
Capture the model/architecture family and any key implementation details needed to reproduce at a high level (e.g., U-Net style, timestep embeddings, data resolution, conditioning choices).
Include the most decision-relevant ablation/sensitivity findings (e.g., effect of variance schedule, parameterization choices, number of steps) and what they imply for implementation choices.
State compute/speed implications: training cost signals (if given), sampling cost/latency implications (slow sampling due to many steps), and whether any faster variants/approximations are discussed.
Summarize qualitative evidence (sample quality, interpolations, failure modes) and tie it to the decision (e.g., does it meet perceived fidelity/diversity requirements?).
If the paper discusses diffusion-as-compression/progressive coding, extract the key claim/algorithmic idea and any quantitative or qualitative tradeoff evidence.

List limitations and risks called out or implied by the evidence (e.g., slow sampling, potential undercoverage of certain details, reliance on schedules/steps), and flag missing figures/tables if relevant.
Provide a concrete go/no-go recommendation with next steps (e.g., implement baseline, choose schedule/steps, evaluate on target dataset/metrics), grounded in the retrieved evidence.
